story.headline: Federal court upholds climate-blockade fines
story.summary: Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court confirmed suspended fines for Extinction Rebellion activists who blockaded a Zurich street in 2021, ruling free expression is no justification.
story.display_body: Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday 26 August that climate activists who blockaded a Zurich street can be criminally punished, holding that freedom of expression is no justification for the blockade. In a series of judgments published Wednesday, the Bundesgericht (the country's highest court) confirmed the suspended fines imposed for coercion (Nötigung) on several Extinction Rebellion activists who, on 4 October 2021, joined roughly 200 protesters occupying central Zurich's Uraniastrasse and sat in the road for about an hour and a half — ignoring repeated police orders to clear it — until police forcibly removed them. The court rejected the activists' argument that their convictions breached their rights to free expression and assembly: it stressed that free expression is a very high value and that authorities must show some tolerance even toward unauthorised gatherings — and noted Zurich police had indeed initially let the protest proceed — but found the activists had "overstepped," because the decisive factors are the scale and duration of a disruption and how severely uninvolved people are affected in their daily lives.
story.why: this sets a national precedent on the limits of protest in Switzerland — demonstrations may be disruptive and inconvenient, but blocking traffic for extended periods gives activists no legal "free pass," a line that will shape how future climate and other protests are policed and prosecuted.

story.headline: EU packaging rules squeeze Swiss exporters
story.summary: The EU's new packaging regulation, in force since 12 August, imposes heavy registration costs on small exporters, including Swiss micro-businesses.
story.display_body: A new EU packaging regulation in force since 12 August is imposing outsized compliance costs on small exporters, Swiss micro-businesses among them, Le Temps reported on Wednesday 26 August. The EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR — the bloc's overhauled rules meant to cut packaging waste and push a "circular economy") now requires sellers shipping goods into EU countries to register, declare and pay fees for the packaging they put on each national market. For very small players the paperwork dwarfs the volumes involved: Patrick Hufschmid, an independent luthier (stringed-instrument maker) based in Aigle (Vaud) who mails guitar plectrums to EU customers in stiff cardboard envelopes, told the paper he now faces close to €260 a year in compliance fees plus separate registrations, declarations and compliance bodies for each country — just to ship under two kilos of cardboard annually to France and Germany.
story.why: Switzerland is outside the EU but its exporters must still meet the bloc's rules to sell there, so an EU regulation aimed at large-scale waste lands as a disproportionate administrative burden on Swiss artisans and micro-enterprises — a concrete example of how EU single-market rules reach across the border into Swiss working life.

story.headline: SBB half-year profit more than doubles
story.summary: Swiss Federal Railways reported a first-half 2026 profit of 126 million francs, up from 48 million a year earlier, with freight breaking even.
story.display_body: Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) reported on Wednesday 26 August that its first-half 2026 profit more than doubled to 126 million francs, from 48 million a year earlier, as ridership rose. An average of 1.45 million passengers travelled with SBB each day in the half; punctuality slipped slightly to 94.1% (down 0.4 points on H1 2025), while customer satisfaction edged up to 80.1 points. The railway credited higher passenger demand, a positive real-estate result and an improved freight performance — SBB Cargo's result rose by 49 million francs to a 2-million-franc profit, its first roughly balanced result in many years. SBB cautioned that its finances remain demanding: to renew its large vehicle fleets and expand service it says it needs a profit of around 500 million francs a year in the medium term to stabilise its debt.
story.why: SBB is a federally owned backbone of Swiss daily life, and the profit jump — set against the much larger sum the company says it actually needs — is a marker of both a recovering post-pandemic demand and the long-term funding gap facing the network reader-taxpayers ultimately underwrite.

story.headline: Islamabad hospital fire kills 14 newborns
story.summary: A fire in a maternity ward at PIMS hospital in Islamabad killed at least 14 infants on Wednesday morning.
story.display_body: A fire in a maternity ward at a public hospital in Islamabad killed at least 14 newborns early on Wednesday 26 August, Pakistani authorities said. The blaze broke out around 6:45 a.m. local time on the third floor — the MCH (maternal and child health) ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) — when, according to rescuers, an air-conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery. Officials said 16 newborns were in the ward at the time and that one was rescued; a nurse read out the names of the dead outside the hospital. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered an immediate investigation.
story.why: it is a catastrophic failure of basic safety in a flagship state hospital, and the death of newborns in a supposedly protected ward points to the fragility of public-health infrastructure in one of the world's most populous countries.

story.headline: Ukraine strikes stall Russian grain exports
story.summary: Intensified Ukrainian drone attacks on Novorossiysk and other Black Sea ports are disrupting Russian grain and oil exports.
story.display_body: Intensified Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia's Black Sea ports are now disrupting Russian grain and oil exports, not just military targets, DW reported on Tuesday 25 August. Strikes in recent weeks on Novorossiysk — Russia's largest commercial Black Sea port and a hub for both grain and crude — have caused significant disruption to shipments, part of a widening Ukrainian campaign against the ports and refineries that fund Moscow's war. Ukraine's deep strikes have already pushed the Russian navy off its former dominance of the northwestern Black Sea; the new element is the reach into commercial export flows.
story.why: Novorossiysk is a major artery for globally traded grain and oil, so a sustained hit to it raises the risk of ripple effects on world food and energy prices — turning a battlefield tactic into a pressure point on markets far from the front.

story.headline: Haiti attack toll rises to 47
story.summary: The UN confirmed at least 47 killed and more than 50 kidnapped in a gang attack near Port-au-Prince on Sunday.
story.display_body: The UN confirmed on Tuesday 25 August that at least 47 people, including at least five children, were killed and more than 50 kidnapped in a gang attack near Haiti's capital — a sharply higher toll than the ~40 first reported. The raid struck Kenscoff, in the hills above Port-au-Prince, on Sunday 23 August; the UN now calls it one of the largest mass kidnappings in the troubled Caribbean country in recent years, and Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack. Survivors, many of them already displaced by earlier violence, fled with whatever belongings they could carry.
story.why: the confirmed scale — and the mass abductions on top of the killings — underscores how far gang control has spread around the Haitian capital and how little protection the state can offer displaced civilians.

story.headline: WHO urges distancing as Ebola spreads in DRC
story.summary: The WHO recommended social-distancing measures in the DRC to counter the country's deadliest recorded Ebola outbreak.
story.display_body: The World Health Organization on Monday 24 August recommended social-distancing measures in the Democratic Republic of Congo to slow the country's deadliest-ever recorded Ebola outbreak. After an emergency-committee meeting last week, WHO director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus issued recommendations that the DRC postpone large gatherings and limit motorcycle taxis to a single passenger in transmission zones, alongside stronger surveillance, case management, community mobilisation and protection of health workers. (Ebola is a severe, often-fatal haemorrhagic fever spread through contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.)
story.why: reaching for social-distancing and mobility limits — tools associated with respiratory pandemics — signals that responders judge case-finding and vaccination alone insufficient to contain this outbreak, and that everyday movement in affected areas is now part of the control strategy.

story.headline: Sunlight makes ammonia from seawater and air
story.summary: An iron-catalysed photochemical cycle fixes nitrogen to ammonia at room temperature using sunlight, in seawater and ambient air.
story.display_body: Making ammonia (NH₃, the basis of nitrogen fertiliser) normally means the Haber–Bosch process — high heat, high pressure, and a large slice of the world's industrial energy. A Bordeaux team instead drives the reaction with light. Cheap iron(II) salts, hit with ultraviolet light, release solvated electrons (free electrons dissolved in the liquid) that reduce a molybdenum catalyst, which grabs N₂ from the air and turns it into ammonia; the spent iron(III) then absorbs more UV, oxidises water and regenerates the iron(II) — closing a self-sustaining loop. They report a 5.0% quantum yield (the fraction of absorbed photons doing useful chemistry) at room temperature and pressure, rising to 10.8% under higher N₂ pressure, and — the notable part — it still runs in unpurified seawater and in ambient air. The whole cycle is genuinely uphill energetically (+329 kJ/mol), light-driven like natural photosynthesis.
story.why: A proof of concept that fertiliser chemistry might one day be powered by sunlight and seawater instead of fossil-fired furnaces — though the modest, UV-limited yields are a long way from a practical process.

story.headline: Physicists film water splitting into hydrogen
story.summary: Femtosecond electron-ion imaging tracks an ionized water molecule forming molecular hydrogen via spontaneous symmetry breaking.
story.display_body: When a water molecule is ionised (an electron knocked out), its two hydrogen atoms can pair up and leave together as molecular hydrogen (H₂) — one of the simplest chemical reactions there is, yet no one had watched the electrons and nuclei move together as it happens. Using correlated electron–ion imaging with few-femtosecond (10⁻¹⁵ s) laser pulses on heavy water (D₂O), backed by simulations, the team reconstructed the full pathway. They find the reaction is indirect, running through three channels with formation times around 34 and 72 femtoseconds, and — the striking result — the molecule must first spontaneously break its own symmetry: only a random, lopsided wobble lets it hop between electronic states at a "conical intersection" (a point where two energy surfaces touch and a molecule can switch states) and fuse the two hydrogens before the oxygen–hydrogen bond finishes breaking.
story.why: A frame-by-frame look at the elementary step behind both radiation damage in water and hydrogen production — showing that even the simplest reactions can hinge on fleeting, spontaneous asymmetry.

story.headline: A recipe to weave magnetic hopfions
story.summary: Simulations turn a toron hosting a monopole-antimonopole pair into knotted 3D magnetic hopfions using an electric current.
story.display_body: The stakes: magnetic hopfions are three-dimensional, knotted textures in a material's spins — a step up in complexity from the flat, whirlpool-like skyrmions already studied as candidate memory bits — and they are predicted to have unusual dynamics, but there is no reliable way to create them on demand. A concrete picture: imagine the atomic spins as tiny compass needles; a hopfion twists their directions into a closed knot that cannot be smoothly undone. This simulation study proposes a clean route: start from a "toron" (a simpler 3D texture that hosts an emergent monopole–antimonopole pair — point-like sources of magnetic field), then run an electric current that annihilates the pair, converting the toron into a hopfion. The starting toron's length sets how many hopfions form, and the current's direction sets the knot's handedness. Honest scope: this is micromagnetic theory only, with no experiment yet — but it hands experimenters concrete control knobs to try.
story.why: If it works on the bench, controllable knotted spin textures could become a new kind of stable, information-carrying object for spintronics.

story.headline: Effective bound for the Zilber-Pink conjecture
story.summary: A paper gives an explicit effective bound and a new finiteness proof for the Zilber-Pink locus of curves in abelian varieties.
story.display_body: The stakes: the Zilber–Pink conjecture is one of the big open problems in arithmetic geometry. It predicts that "unlikely intersections" — rare coincidences where a curve meets special subgroups of a higher-dimensional space more often than plain dimension-counting allows — are finite and controllable, and it would unify and vastly extend classical finiteness theorems (of Manin–Mumford / André–Oort type) about where rational and torsion points can sit. A concrete anchor: picture a winding curve drawn through a grid of "special" points; the conjecture says it can pass through only finitely many of the improbable ones. This work gives an explicit, effective bound on the size of that "Zilber–Pink locus" for curves in abelian varieties after reduction modulo a large prime, plus a fresh proof that the locus is finite. Honest scope: it makes an existing finiteness result effective — you can actually compute the bound — for curves; a concrete advance, not a proof of the full conjecture.
story.why: "Effective" results are the ones that can eventually become algorithms and explicit checks, so pinning down real bounds is how abstract finiteness theorems turn usable.

story.headline: First RAS drug approved for pancreatic cancer
story.summary: The FDA approved daraxonrasib (Rasonque), the first RAS-targeted therapy for metastatic pancreatic cancer, nearly doubling median survival.
story.display_body: On 26 August the US Food and Drug Administration approved daraxonrasib (brand name Rasonque), the first drug to target RAS — the mutated gene that drives roughly 90% of pancreatic tumours — for adults with previously treated metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC, the most common and lethal form). It is a "RAS(ON) multi-selective" inhibitor: rather than blocking a single mutant, it binds the active, switched-on state of several RAS variants at once. In the pivotal Phase 3 RASolute 302 trial (NCT06625320, 500 patients), median overall survival was 13.2 months on the drug versus 6.7 months on standard chemotherapy — close to a doubling. The FDA granted Breakthrough Therapy and Orphan Drug designations and cleared the drug 6.5 months ahead of its review deadline; the most common side effects were rash, diarrhoea, mouth inflammation and nausea.
story.why: RAS was called "undruggable" for four decades, and pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest common cancers, so the first RAS drug to reach it is a genuine milestone — even as absolute median survival stays around 13 months. European relevance: Revolution Medicines says the European Medicines Agency is running an expedited assessment, so a filing here may follow.

story.headline: Shingles vaccine tied to fewer heart events
story.summary: A natural-experiment study links the recombinant shingles vaccine to a 9% lower cardiovascular burden over seven years.
story.display_body: When the US abruptly switched from the older live shingles vaccine to the newer recombinant one (marketed as Shingrix), it created a natural experiment: people vaccinated just before and just after the switch were otherwise similar, which sidesteps the "healthy-vaccinee" bias — healthier people tend to get vaccinated, muddying earlier studies — that has dogged this question. Comparing cardiovascular outcomes in adults aged 60 and over, the Oxford–Birmingham team found the recombinant vaccine was associated with a 9% lower cardiovascular burden over seven years (a "restricted-mean-time-lost" ratio of 0.91, 95% CI 0.88–0.95), with significant reductions in ischaemic heart disease and heart failure in both sexes. The authors are careful: this is observational, the effect is modest and fades over time, and they explicitly call for randomised trials to test whether it is truly causal.
story.why: Shingles vaccination is already recommended for older adults; a real cardiovascular benefit would strengthen that case — but this is an association, not proof, and shouldn't be oversold.

story.headline: 791K genomes map ageing-blood mutations
story.summary: A multi-ancestry GWAS of 791,000 blood genomes maps 81 loci for clonal haematopoiesis using passenger-mutation burden.
story.display_body: Clonal haematopoiesis (CH) — the age-related expansion of blood stem-cell clones — raises the risk of leukaemia, heart disease and death, but most clones carry no known "driver" mutation, so studies that define CH by drivers miss much of it. This team instead counts "passenger" mutations: harmless hitchhiker mutations whose sheer number marks how far a clone has expanded, giving a continuous, more statistically powerful measure. Across 791,067 blood whole-genome sequences from the UK Biobank and the US All of Us program, a multi-ancestry genome-wide association study (GWAS — a scan linking DNA variants to a trait) found 81 genetic loci tied to passenger-mutation burden, 42 of them new, and flagged rare-variant regulators including MBD2, PRKACB and PUF60. Passenger burden itself tracked strongly with later blood cancers and mortality.
story.why: A powerful, driver-free way to study why some people's blood ages faster than others — though as an unreviewed preprint of statistical associations, it needs replication and peer review before any clinical use.

story.headline: Interstellar comet Borisov unlike any on record
story.summary: A full Lowell Observatory dataset shows 2I/Borisov's carbon-chain chemistry surged unlike any of 230 Solar System comets.
story.display_body: 2I/Borisov, discovered in 2019, was the first clearly active comet known to arrive from another star system. A full reduction of Lowell Observatory imaging, spectroscopy and narrowband photometry taken over September–December 2019 finds that its carbon-chain molecules (C₂ and C₃) surged about fourfold relative to cyanide (CN) as it neared the Sun — a trend with distance from the Sun unmatched anywhere in Lowell's 50-year database of 230 comets. Water production peaked at 4.5×10²⁶ molecules per second, with unusually high nitrogen- and hydrogen-bearing ratios, and an almost symmetric gas cloud implying the entire sunlit surface was venting. Set against other groups' data, its chemistry looks unlike any comet born in our own Solar System.
story.why: Comets are frozen leftovers of the systems that made them, so an interstellar one with genuinely alien chemistry is a direct sample of how planet-building differs around other stars. (This is a late, thorough analysis of 2019 data, not a new detection.)

story.headline: Exocomets may water the PDS 70 disc
story.summary: Flickering sodium lines in ESO HARPS data suggest sublimating planetesimals deliver water to the inner disc of PDS 70.
story.display_body: PDS 70 is a young star famous for two planets caught in the act of forming, and JWST recently found water vapour in its inner disc — but where that water comes from was unclear. Mining archival spectra from ESO's HARPS instrument (a high-precision spectrograph in Chile), the team found sodium absorption lines that flicker erratically in strength and velocity from night to night, the fingerprint of dense gas clumps drifting across the star's face. Their favoured explanation: planetesimals (comet- to asteroid-sized bodies) on stretched, plunging orbits that sublimate as they graze the star — "exocomets" — which could be ferrying water inward to the zone where rocky planets form. They stress this is one interpretation among several the data allow.
story.why: It offers a concrete, observable mechanism for delivering water to forming planets — akin to the kind of process that may have helped fill Earth's oceans. European angle: built on ESO/HARPS data with European-led authorship.

story.headline: JWST verdict: exoplanet GJ 1132 b is bare rock
story.summary: A panchromatic JWST+HST transmission spectrum favours no detectable atmosphere on the Earth-sized planet GJ 1132 b.
story.display_body: GJ 1132 b is an Earth-sized planet (1.13 Earth radii) orbiting a small, cool star — exactly the kind of world astronomers most want to test for an atmosphere. Combining JWST, Hubble and ground-based transmission spectra (starlight filtered through any atmosphere during a transit) into one broad 0.71–5.16 micron dataset and running Bayesian atmospheric fits, the authors find that no model with an atmosphere beats a flat, featureless line. A marginal hint of ammonia vanished once a previously flagged, contested JWST visit was excluded. The data favour a bare rock with no detectable atmosphere, though a very thin or hidden one cannot be fully ruled out.
story.why: Whether small planets around small stars can hold onto atmospheres is central to which worlds could be habitable, and each clean "airless" verdict sharpens the picture. (A single-team reanalysis of archival data whose result hinges on one disputed observation.)
